title: Your Plan Might Fail. Your Training Shouldn’t.
html:
Good morning,

The kick came from nowhere.

Well, that's what it felt like.

I'd dropped my guard.

And now I had a chipped tooth.

I'd spent enough time in a dojo to know that punches and kicks were coming. I'd been punched in the face, kicked in the head, the legs and just about everywhere else.

Fortunately, most of it was within the dojo's rules.

But here's the thing that prompted this story.

When someone throws a punch at your face, you don't have time to stop and think about what you're going to do.

You just do it.

You block. You move. You counter.

Sometimes you've already reacted before you've consciously registered what happened.

I've experienced the same thing racing my Peugeot 205 GTI.

I'm no Formula One driver, but I've raced in the European Racing Classics series against some people who make some curious moves on the track.

Someone brakes earlier than expected. Someone moves across your line because they haven't seen you. Someone does something you hadn't anticipated.

And suddenly you're standing on the brakes, steering around them or adjusting your line.

You didn't sit there weighing up your options.

You reacted.

And if you've done it well, you've avoided a crash or made a pass.

Now, here's what I find interesting.

I couldn't possibly have practised every punch someone might throw at me.

And I certainly couldn't have predicted every strange move another racing driver might make.

Yet somehow, I was able to respond to situations I'd never encountered before.

Not always perfectly. That chipped tooth is proof of that.

Mike Tyson famously said, "Everyone has a plan until they get punched in the mouth."

He's right.

But I think there's another side to that.

When you get punched in the face, your plan might go out the window.

But your training doesn't.

All those hours in the dojo. All those laps on the racetrack. All those repetitions.

They've prepared you to respond to things you couldn't possibly have planned for.

And it's not just fighting or racing.

If you're in sales, you're training yourself to handle objections.

If you're a coach, you're preparing for those curly questions.

And if you're trying to change how you react to frustration, criticism or disappointment, you're training for those moments too.

That's one of the things I discovered through my Swearing Project.

I wasn't just trying to stop using certain words.

I was trying to change what came out of my mouth when something went wrong.

Most people think their reactions are automatic. That they can't help what they say or do when something goes wrong.

But I discovered that those reactions can be changed. With practice, a different response can become just as automatic as the old one.

You might not be able to control what life throws at you. But you can train yourself to respond differently when it does.

To your success!

Glenn
